abstract: The force resisting gravity during flight is typically aerodynamic-lift generated by the wings. However, in the smallest insects the low Reynolds number associated with a wing size [≤]1mm reduces the efficiency of using lift for flight. We examined how miniature whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) modulate their flapping kinematics to control flight in the vertical plane. Free-flying whiteflies were recorded using high-speed video cameras, and their 3D wing flapping kinematics were analyzed as a function of flight speed and climb angle. Whiteflies displayed the crescent-shaped wingtip trajectory typical to the drag-utilizing propulsion previously described in other miniature insects. To fly faster, they increased the wing sweep amplitude during the upstroke, resulting in increased wingtip speed relative to the body. To fly at steeper climbing angles the insects oriented their body to direct the upstroke wing motion downwards at a high angle-of-attack. Robotic force measurements confirmed that this downwards rowing in air provides vertical aerodynamic force exceeding body weight at least twofold. To direct the upstroke wing motion into a downwards rowing stroke, the insects used a combination of body pitch and roll that often resulted in the insects flying upside-down. This atypical flight posture emphasizes the adjustments required from tiny insects to convert a flight apparatus that was originally intended for utilizing lift into a drag-utilizing propulsion system, enabling flight at low Reynolds numbers.
